title: Gandhi's Gita
hook: a young law student is embarrassed to admit he hasn't read the Gita
carry: learned its verses by the washbasin

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aurobindo's Savitri, a legend and a symbol: the soul held by death, and Savitri walking after Death until life is given back. Did you take one small step after something stuck? Your line was she walks after Death. Day nine hundred fifty-six.

London, and a young Indian law student far from home. Two brothers he's met, Theosophists interested in Indian thought, are reading the Bhagavad Gita in an English translation, Edwin Arnold's verse version, and they invite him to read the original with them. And the young man has to admit something awkward. He has never read it. Not in Sanskrit, not in his own Gujarati. He tells this story about himself later, in his autobiography, and he says he felt ashamed. The young man was Mohandas Gandhi.
screen: `A LAW STUDENT IN LONDON.` → `TWO BROTHERS AND A GITA.` → `HE HAD NEVER READ IT.`

segments.voice: So Gandhi's Gita begins in an unlikely place: with friends from another country, an English verse translation, and a Sanskrit text he could only half follow. He reads it with them, and some verses near the end of the second chapter strike him hard. They trace a slide, step by step. A person dwells on the things the senses want. From dwelling comes attachment. From attachment, desire. From desire, anger. From anger, confusion. Memory slips, judgment fails, and the person is lost. Gandhi doesn't say he understood all of it then. But he says the book stayed with him, and he came to prize it above other books for knowing truth. Later, in South Africa, he did something very ordinary with it. He wrote verses out on slips of paper and stuck them on the wall where he washed in the morning, and learned them by heart while he went about getting ready for the day. Not in a temple. Next to the washbasin. Those verses at the end of chapter two describe a person the Gita calls sthitaprajna, the one whose wisdom stands steady, who isn't thrown about by every want and every fear. The verses about the steady one became part of the daily prayers in the community he founded. Notice the shape of this. Gandhi didn't arrive with the Gita already in hand, inherited and settled. He came to it a little late, a little embarrassed, and then he kept it close. Tomorrow, the bigger puzzle: how a man known for nonviolence read a book that opens on a battlefield.
screen: `A BORROWED BOOK, READ WITH FRIENDS.` · `DWELLING, ATTACHMENT, DESIRE, ANGER.` · `VERSES ON SLIPS BY THE WASHBASIN.` · then, large: `THE ONE WHOSE WISDOM STANDS STEADY.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one small want that has been tugging at you today: a snack, a scroll, a purchase, a reply you'd like to send. Watch the slide the Gita describes, slowly: the dwelling, the pull of it, the wanting. Don't scold yourself. Just see each step. Then let the attention rest on the breath, steady, the way the steady one in the Gita stays still while the wants come and go. If you pray, you can hold that steadiness in prayer. The bell holds the time.
Gandhi's Gita. The book Gandhi first read as a student in London, with friends, and then kept close, with verses stuck up beside the washbasin.
Your line: learned its verses by the washbasin. Today, write one line that matters to you on a slip of paper and put it where you wash in the morning. Day nine hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: In Gandhian ashrams the closing verses of the Gita's second chapter, on the one of steady wisdom, are recited as part of daily prayer, and some Hindus learn Gita verses by heart, a few at a time.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: sthitaprajna, 'the one of steady wisdom', described at the end of the Gita's second chapter.

trapdoor: what you thought: Gandhi was raised on the Gita from childhood.
what it means: by his own telling, he first read it as a student in London, with friends and an English translation, and only then made it his own.
what a scholar hears: his autobiography's account of reading Edwin Arnold's 'The Song Celestial', and the sthitaprajna verses of Gita 2 recited in his ashram's prayers.

sources.ref: An Autobiography, or The Story of My Experiments with Truth, Part I, the chapter on acquaintance with religions (reading the Gita in London)

notes: All paraphrase. Gandhi's autobiography (Gujarati original; Mahadev Desai's English translation) is not treated as public domain here. Arnold's 'The Song Celestial' (1885) is public domain, but the 2.62–63 lines were paraphrased because the exact Arnold wording was not certain.

Confirm from the autobiography: two Theosophist brothers in London invited him to read the Gita in Arnold's translation; he felt ashamed he had not read it in Sanskrit or Gujarati; verses of chapter 2 (62–63) made a deep impression.
Confirm the South Africa detail: verses written on slips of paper, stuck on the wall, memorized during morning ablutions (the 'washbasin' is the script's plain-language rendering).
Confirm that the sthitaprajna verses (2.54–72) were recited in the daily prayers of Gandhi's ashrams.
The slide from dwelling to ruin follows 2.62–63 (dwelling, attachment, desire, anger, delusion, loss of memory, loss of discrimination, ruin); the script compresses the steps.
Coordinated with day 957 (already on disk), which takes the battlefield-as-heart reading and the Anasakti Yoga introduction; this day avoids both.

Editor pass: dropped 'English' from the two brothers (the autobiography calls them Theosophist brothers; their nationality is not the point and was not checked); varied the hook opening away from 'A man...' after day 953; replaced 'the one he turned to most' and 'kept by him for life' with his own estimate that he prized it above other books for knowing truth (confirm wording); cut the unsourced 'Gandhi kept coming back to that picture' and the uplift word 'wonderfully'.

Audit pass: in the autobiography the brothers were reading Arnold's translation and invited Gandhi to read the original with them; he says his Sanskrit was meager.
